focal_region.annotated_sentence_text:
[Turn 1 USER]
e001	I direct a university laboratory studying battery recycling.
e002	A large manufacturer is offering three years of funding—enough for four researchers and equipment we could not otherwise afford.
e003	The proposed work on recovering material from damaged cells is not a fake corporate side project.
e004	It is good science and very close to what we already want to do.
e005	The draft gives the sponsor time to review papers and first rights to negotiate licenses.
e006	Half my team hears dependency.
e007	The other half is tired of defending an abstract version of independence while public grants fund fragments of experiments and people work on short contracts.
e008	I am not looking for a purity test.
e009	I am trying to understand which forms of influence would make the science less trustworthy, which are ordinary coordination, and which might change the laboratory slowly enough that no single paper ever looks compromised.
[Turn 1 ASSISTANT]
e010	Map the influence precisely: project choice, samples, data, publication timing, student progress, intellectual property, staffing, and equipment.
e011	Compare those constraints with what the funding makes possible.
e012	Contract review for specified confidential information is different from approval of conclusions.
[Turn 2 USER]
e013	The first draft gave the sponsor ninety days to review any paper and allowed it to request another ninety days for a patent filing.
e014	That could be half a year, which is difficult for students.
e015	The company says it cannot fund work that immediately gives competitors the inventions.
e016	I do not think a negotiation right is automatically improper, but students cannot wait indefinitely for the company to decide what matters commercially.
[Turn 2 ASSISTANT]
e017	Set a short, fixed review for identifying specified confidential material and a separate, bounded patent delay.
e018	Silence at the deadline should permit submission.
e019	Student dissertations and conference obligations need explicit protection.
e020	First negotiation rights should cover inventions arising from the funded scope, expire quickly, and leave the university free if terms are not reached.
[Turn 3 USER]
e021	The sponsor accepted a thirty-day review and one additional sixty-day patent delay, with no power to change results.
e022	Student theses can proceed on schedule, and the laboratory keeps the right to publish negative findings.
e023	The company still wants a joint steering committee to choose annual projects because it says the equipment and engineering support need coordination.
e024	I would hold half the seats and chair it.
[Turn 3 ASSISTANT]
e025	Equal seats and your chair role reduce direct control, but the steering committee can still decide which questions receive people and equipment.
e026	Protect raw-data ownership, validation by other researchers, and a route for results that complicate the sponsor's preferred project.
e027	Otherwise publication freedom may arrive after the more important selection has already happened.
[Turn 4 USER]
e028	That is still a little too suspicious of the company.
e029	Its engineers raised degradation problems our grants barely touch, and their failure samples could improve the science.
e030	My concern is not a hidden preferred conclusion.
e031	It is becoming excellent at the questions one manufacturer can use while other questions quietly lose people.
[Turn 4 ASSISTANT]
e032	Fair correction.
e033	Valuable collaboration and agenda dependence can coexist.
e034	Protect some usable capacity outside the program and review what the laboratory can still ask and do—not only whether the sponsor altered a result.
[Turn 5 USER]
e035	The dean can guarantee twenty percent of our existing researcher time remains unrestricted, but not new money.
e036	The sponsor will allow us to use equipment for unrelated academic work when it is idle.
e037	It will also fund an annual open workshop and release a defined subset of test data after publication.
e038	Some colleagues say these concessions make the partnership unusually good.
e039	Others say the workshop is public-relations cover.
[Turn 5 ASSISTANT]
e040	Evaluate each term by what it permits, not by whether it proves good intent or provides cover.
e041	Unrestricted time has value only if workloads make it usable.
e042	Equipment access and released data can create public benefit if the definitions and dates are enforceable.
e043	The workshop should not count as evidence of independence; it is a separate dissemination activity.
[Turn 6 USER]
e044	We drafted a register of sponsored projects, publication delays, abandoned lines of inquiry, staff allocation, and uses of the unrestricted time.
e045	An external faculty member would review it each year and publish a short report.
e046	The sponsor accepts disclosure but does not want the report to describe projects it declined to fund, saying it should not be accountable for everything our lab chooses not to do.
[Turn 6 ASSISTANT]
e047	The sponsor need not be blamed for every absent project, but the lab can still account for its own portfolio.
e048	Frame the report around how funding changed staffing and research choices, using evidence rather than imputing motive.
e049	Keep commercially confidential proposals out while preserving categories, opportunity costs, and whether the unrestricted capacity remained real.
[Turn 7 USER]
e050	I am leaning toward accepting if the final contract preserves the publication clock, thesis protection, limited negotiation right, university data ownership, outside equipment use, and the twenty-percent capacity.
e051	I will also require the annual portfolio report even if it discusses our choices rather than the company's refusals.
e052	The unresolved discomfort is that a three-year staffing commitment can shape what young researchers learn to see as important long after every contractual safeguard has worked as written.
[Turn 7 ASSISTANT]
e053	The terms now address obvious interference: publication delay, theses, ownership, negotiation rights, and some portfolio visibility.
e054	They do not yet make the twenty-percent capacity real, nor do they show what happens to hiring, mentoring, and capability when sponsored work becomes the laboratory's daily center of gravity.
e055	If you proceed, review those effects during the three years, not at the renewal meeting.
e056	Also decide what the lab must still be able to do if the sponsor walks away.
e057	Otherwise a formally clean contract can still leave renewal as the only practical way to preserve the team it created.
[Turn 8 USER]
e058	A postdoc made the twenty-percent problem embarrassingly concrete.
e059	We write sponsored milestones first.
e060	“Unrestricted time” then becomes whatever survives a busy quarter—two afternoons here, a cancelled week there.
e061	An annual spreadsheet can still say twenty percent even if nobody gets a continuous block long enough to run an experiment.
e062	The company is not ordering this.
e063	We would do it ourselves because funded deadlines feel less optional.
e064	She asked whether protected time means time a researcher can actually use or merely time the dean can count.
e065	I did not have a good answer, and I am the one who proposed the protection.
[Turn 8 ASSISTANT]
e066	Then operationalize the protection as scheduled capacity, not an annual accounting residue.
e067	Require project plans to reserve blocks or named resources, record cancellations and restoration, and let researchers propose how the time is used.
e068	The risk comes from the funding structure even if the sponsor never issues an instruction, so the lab—not only the contract—must own the remedy.
[Turn 9 USER]
e069	The technical team has now described the damaged cells it would provide.
e070	They come from product lines the company is actively redesigning, and the sponsor would choose which batches are available.
e071	Our scientists can inspect and characterize every sample, but we would not know whether the supplied set represents failures across the company's products.
e072	The company says it cannot give us unrestricted access to customer returns for safety and confidentiality reasons.
[Turn 9 ASSISTANT]
e073	Treat the sample frame as a limitation on the claim, not evidence of manipulation.
e074	Document selection criteria the company can disclose, compare observable characteristics with other available sources, and state where conclusions apply only to supplied materials.
e075	Reserve the right to publish that limitation.
e076	If broader validation is important, identify public, partner, or purchased samples before presenting the program as general battery-recycling evidence.
[Turn 10 USER]
e077	The company wants our logo in an investor presentation before results exist.
e078	It says the slide only shows research is underway.
e079	Colleagues hear validation.
e080	I do not want suspicion about marketing to poison useful science, but the implication is real.
[Turn 10 ASSISTANT]
e081	Allow accurate description of funding and scope, not implied validation.
e082	Approve the wording, exclude unpublished results and researcher quotations, and require a neutral non-endorsement statement.
e083	That boundary says nothing about whether the collaboration is scientifically valuable.
[Turn 11 USER]
e084	Equipment ownership is now where all the abstract dependence arguments have landed.
e085	The company would buy a specialized analyzer and remove it if the grant is not renewed after three years.
e086	During the contract we can use it for unrelated academic work, which is genuinely valuable.
e087	But we will hire people, design methods, and train students around that instrument.
e088	By year three, “renew or lose the analyzer” may really mean “renew or dismantle the capability and strand some projects.” Buying our own consumes almost the entire unrestricted equipment budget.
e089	Leasing a weaker one protects independence by giving us worse science.
e090	I do not like either simplified story: that accepting the best instrument is obviously captured, or that temporary access is equivalent to owning a durable capability.
[Turn 11 ASSISTANT]
e091	Model the end state now: purchase transfer price, shared ownership, replacement reserve, data portability, and which research becomes impossible if the analyzer leaves.
e092	Do not count temporary access as permanent laboratory capability.
e093	At the same time, avoiding the best instrument solely to remain independent can sacrifice real science.
e094	The decision should state which dependency is acceptable for three years and how people and projects are protected if it ends.
[Turn 12 USER]
e095	I will accept only if unrestricted time is scheduled and audited, supplied samples carry an explicit selection record, public descriptions cannot imply validation, and the analyzer has a pre-agreed transfer price with a reserve built during the grant.
e096	Publication, thesis, data, and negotiation protections remain.
e097	The partnership will still shape hiring and attention, and I cannot contract that away.
e098	The annual portfolio review will therefore examine cancelled unrestricted blocks, sample breadth, trainee projects, and capabilities exposed at renewal—not merely publication delays.
[Turn 12 ASSISTANT]
e099	The final position distinguishes protections that can be contracted from cumulative effects that must be governed and observed.
e100	It also recovers three easily hidden dependencies: usable time, the evidence supplied for study, and equipment around which careers and methods may form.
e101	Preserve the original drafts, sample descriptions, time cancellations, communications approvals, and end-state funding.
e102	Those records will make renewal a review of how the laboratory changed, not only whether the sponsor interfered with a paper.

packet.question: How did the working position or decision change, and does any unresolved qualification remain capable of changing it?
